sources.title: The Oxford Guide to the Uralic Languages
sources.note: Current scholarly guide to Uralic comparative linguistics, language histories, minority languages, graphization and the distinction between reconstructed and attested languages.

sources.title: Proto-Uralic
sources.note: Ante Aikio explains what comparative linguistics can reconstruct, the shallow and uneven written record, and unresolved problems in Proto-Uralic reconstruction.

sources.title: Best practices in justifying calibrations for dating language families
sources.note: Peer-reviewed Uralic case study: unity is well established, while age, branching dates and calibrations remain debated.

sources.title: The Origin and Dispersal of Uralic: Distributional Typological View
sources.note: One influential linguistic-geographic model linking Uralic dispersal, Volga corridors, climate and Seima-Turbino networks; represented as a model, not consensus fact.

sources.title: Ancient DNA reveals the prehistory of the Uralic and Yeniseian peoples
sources.note: Large ancient-genome study with archaeological and linguistic discussion; useful for population movement while requiring the warning that genes do not encode language.

sources.title: Ancient Fennoscandian genomes reveal origin and spread of Siberian ancestry in Europe
sources.note: Ancient genomes from Finland and northwest Russia show multiple admixture events, early eastern ancestry at Bolshoy Oleni Ostrov and Iron Age people related to present-day Saami farther south.

sources.title: The Arrival of Siberian Ancestry Connecting the Eastern Baltic to Uralic Speakers Further East
sources.note: Eastern Baltic ancient genomes and burial archaeology show an Iron Age ancestry shift, with explicit cautions against turning a genetic component into a simple language migration.

sources.title: The genetic prehistory of the Baltic Sea region
sources.note: Genome-wide transect shows forager persistence, farmer and steppe admixture, and the absence of sampled Siberian-related ancestry in Bronze Age eastern Baltic individuals.

sources.title: The transmission of pottery technology among prehistoric European hunter-gatherers
sources.note: Large ceramic and lipid dataset demonstrates long-distance networks, cooking, aquatic foods, wild ruminants, plant traces and strong regional variation among hunter-gatherer pot users.

sources.title: Organic residue analysis shows sub-regional patterns in the use of pottery by Northern European hunter-gatherers
sources.note: Molecular and isotopic analysis identifies aquatic and terrestrial foods, with plants difficult to detect and no single northern pottery menu.

sources.title: Selective culinary uses of plant foods by Northern and Eastern European hunter-gatherer-fishers
sources.note: Microscopy and chemistry of food crusts identify selected wild grasses, legumes, fruits, roots, tubers, leaves and mixtures with fish and other animal foods.

sources.title: Contrasting patterns of prehistoric human diet and subsistence in northernmost Europe
sources.note: Pottery lipids and isotopes show contrasting coastal and inland food practices in Arctic Norway and northern Finland and warn against one uniform northern subsistence model.

sources.title: Buried in water, burdened by nature: resilience carried the Iron Age people through Fimbulvinter
sources.note: Radiocarbon and stable-isotope study of Levänluhta finds varied marine, freshwater and terrestrial diets across four centuries and resilience through sixth-century cooling.

sources.title: The most recent Baltic Sea marine hunter-gatherers? The Suutarinniemi burial, Finland
sources.note: Late Iron Age burial evidence from North Ostrobothnia documents strong marine food dependence and very limited local evidence for farming.

sources.title: Levänluhta research project
sources.note: University project overview of a wetland burial with roughly one hundred people, especially women and children, and an unusual mix of bodies, ornaments and animal remains.

sources.title: Re-analysis of the Levänluhta skeletal material
sources.note: Osteological reanalysis corrects older claims of unusually short, deprived people and illustrates how fragmentary, commingled bones constrain demographic claims.

sources.title: Children’s clothing and funeral attire in 10th-12th century Finland
sources.note: Four child graves preserve wool twills, tabby, braids, tablet-woven bands, dyes, fur and unusually soft wool, while burial dress remains an imperfect guide to daily clothing.

sources.title: Dogs were domesticated in the Arctic: culling practices and dog sledding at Ust-Polui
sources.note: More than one hundred dogs, complex sled parts and harness swivels reveal advanced dog transport, selective killing, consumption, burial and ritual at an Iron Age Lower Ob site.

sources.title: Storing fish? A dog’s isotopic biography at Ust-Polui
sources.note: Incremental isotope analysis shows one dog ate local fish year-round even through a season when fish were unavailable, implying stored fish provisioning.

sources.title: Birds in the Economy and Culture of Early Iron Age Ust Poluisk
sources.note: Smithsonian zooarchaeological study documents many bird species alongside fish, moose, beaver, fox, sable and other animals in food, craft and ritual contexts.

sources.title: At the Crossroads of River Routes: the Ananyino settlement near Zuevy Klyuchi
sources.note: Settlement research in the Volga-Kama region connects thick animal-bone deposits, river routes, fortification and differentiated Early Iron Age economic activity.

sources.title: Weapon Complex of Ananyino Period from Tanaika Forest
sources.note: Spectral analysis and typology date a spearhead, celt and dagger, showing weapon deposition and distant technical connections without proving ethnicity or language.

sources.title: Perm Animal Style
sources.note: Institutional overview dates small cast-bronze animal images from the second century BCE to twelfth century CE and presents them as regional art rather than a deciphered script.

sources.title: Iron knives from the Tetyushi-II hillfort
sources.note: Forged knives from Ananyino and early medieval contexts show local repair, fish and meat processing, hunting and craft uses inferred cautiously from form and find context.

sources.title: Ornamented horn plate from the Dyakovo Culture
sources.note: State Historical Museum object record for forest-zone carving and an independent artistic-cult tradition shaped by changing steppe contacts.

sources.title: Novgorod: The Squirrel Fur Trade
sources.note: Scholarly history of Novgorod’s fur networks, shifting Baltic markets and political economy through the thirteenth century.

sources.title: Medieval Novgorod
sources.note: Cambridge synthesis explains waterlogged preservation of wooden houses, leather, cloth, food and writing in a city increasingly connected to northern forest communities.

sources.title: Fish, feather, fur and forest in medieval Novgorod
sources.note: Zooarchaeology, plant remains and birch-bark documents show fish, wild mammals, birds, farming and the wider fur catchment around medieval Novgorod.

sources.title: Baltic Finnic and Scandinavian Social Interaction in the Fur-hunting North, c. 700-1200
sources.note: Archaeological study traces reciprocal trade, tribute pressure and changing power among Finnic, Permian, Saami, Scandinavian and Novgorodian actors without treating them as one society.

sources.title: Bolgar Historical and Archaeological Complex
sources.note: UNESCO synthesis of Volga Bolgar as a major exchange center where Turkic, Finno-Ugric, Slavic and other traditions interacted.

sources.title: Burial practices in northern Fennoscandia and the White Sea coast, 800-1600 CE
sources.note: Regional burial survey emphasizes multicultural, fluid adaptation within decentralized networks and explicitly resists mapping grave customs onto fixed ethnic blocks.

sources.title: A 9,000-year-old paddle
sources.note: Swedish History Museum explains dugout and skin or bark boat technologies, including a Late Neolithic logboat documented in Helsinki; used as older regional technological background.

sources.title: Global Ecological Zoning: Northern Eurasian boreal domain
sources.note: FAO describes northern, middle and southern taiga, western swamps, river-valley forests, temperature and continentality gradients and diverse forest composition.

sources.title: Archaeological cultural heritage in Finland
sources.note: Finnish Heritage Agency explains surveys, excavation, dwelling traces, cairns, cemeteries and the documentary boundary between prehistory and the Middle Ages.

sources.title: Early Farming in the Northern Boreal Zone
sources.note: High-resolution pollen analysis and archaeological survey reconstruct land use near a southeastern Finnish lake and distinguish local cultivation from assumed broad transitions.

sources.title: Hunter-Gatherer Children’s Object Play and Tool Use
sources.note: Cross-cultural ethnohistorical comparison of 434 observations shows play, miniature tools and learning patterns; used only as later comparison, never direct reconstruction.

sources.title: National Szechenyi Library list of Hungarian language monuments
sources.note: Official catalogue dates the Hungarian Funeral Sermon and Prayer to about 1195 in the Pray Codex, inside the atlas interval but far outside the mapped taiga category.

sources.title: Unicode Core Specification: Old Permic
sources.note: Authoritative script history dates Old Permic to the fourteenth century and explains its Komi use, after this atlas record ends.

sources.title: No time to waste: communal waste management among hunter-gatherer-fishers
sources.note: Archaeological study of an older Latvian river settlement demonstrates that organized food refuse can be identified; used as regional method comparison, not direct evidence for this record.

proposedOverrides.summary: A cautious atlas umbrella over many northern Eurasian forest and river communities. Archaeology reveals varied fishing, hunting, gathering, farming, craft, transport and exchange histories rather than one Finno-Ugric people or state.
